articles.title: Pakistan textile exporters warn EU-India trade deal could erode market advantage - Arab News PK
articles.summary: Pakistan textile exporters warn EU-India trade deal could erode market advantage  Arab News PK
articles.full_text:
- SITE industry chief warns rising production costs could undermine Pakistan’s textile export growth
- India’s trade agreement with EU could take effect in early 2027, narrowing Pakistan’s tariff advantage
KARACHI: Pakistan’s textile exporters risk losing their competitive advantage in European markets as improved trade access for rival countries and rising production costs threaten the sector, a leading industry representative warned on Saturday, urging the government to lower manufacturing costs and pursue new export markets.
The warning comes as the European Union prepares to implement a free trade agreement with India that could reduce Pakistan’s relative tariff advantage under the bloc’s Generalized Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+). India and the EU concluded negotiations in January, and India’s trade minister said on Thursday the agreement could become operational in early 2027.
SITE Association of Industry (SAI) President Abdul Hadi said Pakistan’s textile and apparel exports had grown in the first quarter of the current fiscal year, but high operating costs and increasing regional competition threatened to undermine further gains.
“Exports rose 5.26pc year-on-year to $5.026 billion in the first quarter of FY27, but rising production costs and competition from regional exporters could undermine this growth,” Hadi said in a statement, citing industry figures.
Pakistan’s textile and clothing industry is the country’s largest export sector and a major source of employment and foreign exchange earnings. The European Union is among its most important markets, with preferential access under GSP+ allowing a substantial share of Pakistani goods to enter the bloc duty-free.
Hadi said Pakistan could not rely indefinitely on existing trade preferences and needed to improve productivity, product quality and industrial efficiency to remain competitive.
He urged the government to strengthen trade diplomacy, secure access to additional export markets and reduce the cost of doing business.
According to figures cited by the association, Pakistan’s textile and apparel exports reached approximately $18 billion in the fiscal year ending June 2026. The sector accounts for around 60 percent of the country’s export earnings, the association said.
Hadi said Pakistan remained heavily dependent on relatively low-value-added products, including yarn, fabric and basic home textiles, limiting its ability to earn higher returns in international markets.
He called for greater investment in technical textiles, branded apparel and other higher-margin products, alongside modern technology and improvements in manufacturing productivity.
The SITE chief also expressed concern over declining domestic cotton production, which he said had increased the textile industry’s dependence on imported raw materials.
He also urged the government to improve domestic cotton production and strengthen coordination between the agricultural and industrial sectors to ensure a reliable supply of quality raw materials at competitive prices.

articles.title: China Imposes Export Control on Tunnel Boring Machines in What Indian Expert Calls ‘Covert Trade War’ - Vision Times
articles.summary: China Imposes Export Control on Tunnel Boring Machines in What Indian Expert Calls ‘Covert Trade War’  Vision Times
articles.full_text:
Citing national security interests, China’s Ministry of Commerce said in an announcement on Oct. 19 that it was imposing export controls on tunnel-boring machines and related items destined for “sensitive countries” and regions with which China has disputes. An Indian expert described the move as a surprise and a “secret trade war” and called for a comprehensive response from New Delhi.
“China will impose export controls on full-face tunnel-boring machines, including earth-pressure-balance, slurry-balance and other shield machines, as well as open, single-shield and double-shield rock tunnel-boring machines,” the ministry said in a release on Monday, Oct. 20.
India and China share a long, disputed border along the Himalayan mountain range, which separates the Tibetan Plateau from the Indian subcontinent. Following the deadly 2020 Galwan Valley clash, in which soldiers from both countries were killed, India and China accelerated infrastructure development along the border, including the construction of roads, railways, tunnels and bridges.
This is where China’s export controls on heavy equipment and machinery become geopolitically sensitive. According to the official announcement, the controls cover machines designed for use at altitudes above 3,000 meters.
The controls also cover specified engines, motors, compressors, chassis, folding arms and related hydraulic and pumping technologies. Exports of these items to “sensitive countries and regions with which China has disputes” require an export license from the Ministry of Commerce, according to the announcement.

Expert: This is ‘China’s unannounced covert trade war with India’
Banuchandar Nagarajan, an Indian public policy adviser, told Vision Times that “the latest export ban or export restrictions on tunnel-boring machines are part of China’s unannounced, covert trade war with India,”
“They inflict a double whammy: on one side, they restrict access to critical minerals and components, making it difficult to manufacture machines and tools in India. On the other side, they also impose restrictions on finished products.”
In an August 2025 parliamentary response in the Lok Sabha, India’s Ministry of Commerce and Industry confirmed that China’s export controls on rare-earth magnets had caused supply-chain bottlenecks affecting Indian industries, including electric vehicle (EV) manufacturers, the Press Trust of India (PTI) reported.
Nagarajan said such restrictions had occurred many times before, including restrictions involving carbide tools—industrial cutting, drilling and machining tools made primarily from cemented carbide, a high-performance composite material.
“There is a restriction on tungsten carbide exports to India, and at the same time, they keep dumping low-cost tools into India, thereby hurting our local manufacturers.
“Unfortunately, even the government has turned a blind eye to this when it comes to procurement, where government bids are based on L1 [lowest bidder] and not the total cost of ownership,” he said.
Nagarajan called for a “comprehensive” response from Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s administration and outlined four measures that should form its basis.
“First, the critical minerals partnership, on which the government is already taking steps. Second, making sure that we develop these advanced manufacturing capabilities so that we produce these machines as part of Atmanirbhar Bharat.”
Atmanirbhar Bharat, meaning “self-reliant India,” is an initiative launched by Modi in May 2020 to strengthen domestic manufacturing, reduce excessive dependence on imports and make the country more resilient to global supply-chain disruptions.
“Third, we make sure that we have anti-dumping import controls on Chinese goods. Fourth, government entities and PSUs don’t procure Chinese goods just because they are cheap based on L1 bids,” Nagarajan said.
Meanwhile, Indian government officials have said they would consult industry stakeholders on an appropriate response to China’s export controls on heavy equipment and machinery, including tunnel-boring machines and related items. They have also ruled out any significant impact on highway construction in India, according to The Economic Times, a major Indian daily.

articles.title: Trump Says US Is Close to Trade Deals with Mexico and Canada as Tariff Talks Advance - Sri Lanka Guardian
articles.summary: Trump Says US Is Close to Trade Deals with Mexico and Canada as Tariff Talks Advance  Sri Lanka Guardian
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington was close to reaching a trade agreement with Mexico and that negotiations with Canada were also progressing, as the three North American countries seek to resolve tensions over tariffs and trade rules.
“We are close to reaching an agreement with Mexico. It will be a very good agreement, hopefully for them too, but it will certainly be a good agreement for us,” Trump said at the White House before travelling to Fort Myer, Florida, for an election rally. He said Canada was also working hard to secure a deal with the United States.
“Although I hate to say it, we have all the cards in our favour in both cases,” he added.
The negotiations centre on a framework to reduce tariffs affecting the automotive and steel industries, both important to the economies of Mexico and Canada. The talks have gained urgency since Washington announced in July that it would not renew the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA), which Trump signed during his first presidency in 2020.
Negotiations between Washington and Mexico City accelerated after media reports last week suggested that discussions had stalled because of opposition from US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. According to The Wall Street Journal, the two countries had been close to an agreement under which the United States would reduce tariffs on steel, aluminium and automobiles in exchange for concessions from Mexico. Disagreements over duties on vehicles and metals reportedly prevented the deal from advancing.
Trump has sought to portray the remaining differences as manageable. Speaking at an election rally in Kansas on Monday, he said the United States would not lose $150 billion through its trade deficit with Mexico. Referring to the deficit, he declared that Washington was close to a major agreement that could reduce the figure dramatically, “maybe to zero”.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said on Tuesday that the countries were also “very close” to an agreement, while stressing that several issues remained unresolved. She said Washington wanted to rebalance trade, whereas Mexico was seeking the greatest possible reduction in existing tariffs on vehicles, steel and aluminium, as well as assurances that no additional duties would be imposed.
“There are still issues that we have not fully resolved because we want what is best for Mexico,” Sheinbaum said. She added that the US administration had shown a constructive attitude towards the negotiations.
The three countries have spent months discussing arrangements to replace the USMCA, which Trump described during his first term as the best trade agreement in history. Since returning to the White House for a second term, however, he has pursued changes to trade rules intended to benefit US industries. The countries have consequently shifted towards bilateral negotiations.
Mexican officials remain optimistic that an agreement can be reached before the end of the year. Economy Secretary Marcelo Ebrard said last week that he hoped to secure more flexible US tariffs on Mexican vehicle and steel exports.
The automotive sector is particularly concerned about the 25% US tariff on vehicles that fail to meet the USMCA’s rules of origin. Under the existing agreement, 75% of a vehicle’s components must originate in North America for it to qualify for tariff-free treatment. Washington wants to raise that threshold to about 82%, while also demanding that half of the components come from US factories. The proposals are intended to exclude Chinese and European components but would impose additional requirements on manufacturers operating across the region.
Mexico also faces a 50% US tariff on steel under Section 232 of US trade law, alongside a general 10% tariff imposed on the country under Section 301.
Sheinbaum’s government has pursued high-level diplomatic discussions to secure tariff reductions without derailing negotiations. As a gesture of goodwill, Mexico has temporarily suspended its 10% tariff on imported automotive components, even as it continues pressing Washington to ease restrictions on its exports.

articles.title: China banned TBM exports, but India is building its own tunnel boring machines; Ashwini Vaishnaw shares pr - The Economic Times
articles.summary: China banned TBM exports, but India is building its own tunnel boring machines; Ashwini Vaishnaw shares pr  The Economic Times
articles.full_text:
Listen to this article in summarized format
In separate social media posts on Thursday, Vaishnaw highlighted the engineering challenges involved in the Rishikesh-Karnaprayag railway project and the country's efforts to develop a complete domestic TBM ecosystem, from design and manufacturing to maintenance.
Rishikesh-Karnaprayag railway line: 83% of the route will pass through tunnels
The 125-km Rishikesh-Karnaprayag railway line is being built through difficult Himalayan terrain and is expected to improve connectivity to several parts of Uttarakhand.
Read more - In 75 hours, India’s longest train journey takes you across 4,188 km, from Assam’s tea gardens to Kanyakumari’s coastline; watch viral video
Describing the project on X, Vaishnaw said, “Engineering through the Himalayas! 125 km, 12 stations, 83% tunnels. The Rishikesh-Karnaprayag rail line is not just a track, it's Uttarakhand's lifeline to the future.”
The project includes 16 tunnels and 19 bridges, with around 104 km of the alignment passing through tunnels. The minister described the route as a demanding engineering undertaking shaped by the region's geological conditions.
Why building tunnels in the Himalayas is difficult
One of the major challenges is the geology of the Young Fold Mountains, where sections of the terrain contain softer material rather than solid granite. Under pressure, the surrounding ground can squeeze inwards after a tunnel is bored, complicating construction.
Vaishnaw said engineers carried out extensive investigations before deciding to use TBMs on the project. The machines were then modified to handle the conditions.
“When the decision to use a Tunnel Boring Machine (TBM) was taken for this Karnaprayag project, extensive investigations were carried out beforehand. If a tunnel is bored through solid rock strata, it does not squeeze. However, in soft strata, the tunnel has a tendency to squeeze inward. By modelling this squeezing tendency, modifications were engineered into the Tunnel Boring Machine,” he said.
The changes included modifications to the cutter head and the shield that houses the segmental lining assembly. Engineers also made changes to the drive system to provide additional torque and thrust.
“Numerous modifications were made to the cutter head. Following that, significant modifications were also made to the shield where the segmental lining plate assembly is housed. A special design was implemented in its drive system to deliver extra torque and extra thrust. Due to this specialised design, the Tunnel Boring Machine has proven successful in the Rishikesh–Karnaprayag project,” the minister added.
Rishikesh-Karnaprayag railway project: Latest work status
Vaishnaw said construction has reached an advanced stage across most sections, with tunnels T-1 and T-5 among the key stretches where work continues.
Tunnel T-1, which is 11 km long, is particularly challenging because of the difficult geology and the presence of human settlements along the stretch. Micropiles are being used to stabilise the area, he said.
“Tunnel 1 is the most complex section. It spans 11 kilometres. It is the most complex because the geology here is the most difficult. Several tunnels ahead have already been completed. There is also considerable human habitation in this stretch, so micropiles are being utilised to stabilise the area. Overall, the progress on this project is very good... Work on T-5 and T-1 is also progressing at a rapid pace,” he said.
The stations listed along the route include Shivpuri, Byasi, Devprayag, Janasu, Maletha, Srinagar, Dhari Devi, Tilani, Gholtir, Gauchar and Karnaprayag.
How the railway line could improve access to Uttarakhand's pilgrimage sites
Once completed, the railway line is expected to make journeys towards Karnaprayag and Rudraprayag easier and improve access to pilgrimage destinations such as Kedarnath and Badrinath.
The project also has strategic significance because Karnaprayag, its terminal station, is around 123 km from the India-China border, according to Vaishnaw.
The line is intended to strengthen connectivity in the hill state, where road journeys can be affected by mountainous terrain and challenging travel conditions.
India aims to manufacture TBMs larger than 16 metres
Alongside the railway project, the government is working to expand India's domestic capacity to manufacture the machines needed for major tunnelling projects.
Vaishnaw said TBMs are essential for the country's expanding infrastructure programme, which includes railways, highways and power projects. India previously relied on imports, but domestic manufacturing has progressed to machines with 8-metre and 15-metre diameters.
“With the vast amount of infrastructure currently being built across the country, whether for railways, highways, or power, these various infrastructure projects heavily rely on Tunnel Boring Machines (TBMs). There was a time when all tunnel boring machines had to be imported,” he said.
“But now, all 8-meter diameter tunnel boring machines are being manufactured in India. Moreover, even 15-meter tunnel boring machines have now started being made in India. There is a TBM plant in Tamil Nadu. And very soon, TBMs with a diameter exceeding 16 meters will also be manufactured in India. This means India is becoming self-reliant (Aatmanirbhar) in TBMs, right from design and manufacturing to maintenance,” the minister added.
He said the development of domestic manufacturing and technical expertise was part of the Aatmanirbhar Bharat vision.
“The country is also preparing to manufacture TBMs with diameters exceeding 16 metres,” Vaishnaw said in a separate post.
With larger machines planned for domestic production, India is seeking to build a more complete TBM ecosystem and reduce dependence on imported technology for major infrastructure projects.
